utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. You may be seated. Good morning, everybody. Good morning the members of the Prosecution, members of the Defence. We are here to resume our work. I believe we shall have some delay because certain things have to be regulated but we are all here and we are waiting, but I believe that now we do have our videolink established and it will be Mr. Deretic who will tell us who will be his witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. Zigic's Defence has envisaged three witnesses for today. The first witness is Dr. Dusanka Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see here on the monitor the name of Dusanka Andjelkovic. Good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I believe that a representative of the Registrar has a solemn declaration and I shall be very happy to hear you pronounce your solemn declaration. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, Dusanka Andjelkovic, solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you may be seated, Doctor. I also think that the representative of the Registrar who is with you has a piece of paper with your name. I think you will be given a pseudonym and now I should like to ask Madam Registrar to tell us which is this witness's pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D49 -- D9/4, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is D9/4. Is that it? D9/4?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can Melinda, who is there with you, that is the representative of the Registrar, will you please give this piece of paper to the witness so that she can confirm that it is indeed her name and her pseudonym? Has everything been prepared there? Very well. We obviously still have a problem of translation. I said, Madam Registrar, are the things -- were things prepared properly with Ms. Melinda over there? That is, do they have a piece of paper prepared with the name of the doctor, Dusanka Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, Melinda does have all the names of the witnesses and she will prepare the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am now asking Melinda to show the witness a piece of paper with her name on it so as to establish if Dr. Dusanka Andjelkovic -- will she tell us yes or no, whether it is -- no, I don't think it is necessary. Right. The pseudonym for this witness will be D4/9 [as interpreted]. Right. Witness, thank you very much for coming and now you will answer questions that Mr. Deretic will ask you. Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not want to interrupt, but as far as I know, we did not ask for any protection, nor did we ask for a pseudonym for Dr. Andjelkovic because we do not think there is any need for it. I'm saying this merely to facilitate our work today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, perhaps I mixed things up. Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Examined by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind and give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Dusanka Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I was born on the 31st of July 1942 in Varazdin in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I do. I have a daughter and two granddaughters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind and tell us what is your ethnicity and your religion.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I am a Serb and orthodox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have already mentioned that you are a physician, but are you also specialised in something?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. I am a specialist in epidemiology, and I am the chief physician in a hospital and doctor of medical sciences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your job and where do you work?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I deal with epidemiology, that is, the whole protection of the population, control of the state of health of the population, implementation of prophylactic and preventive measures, combating infectious and uninfectious disease, hygienic conditions of the population in general; therefore, my jurisdiction is society as such as a whole rather than individual patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, in June 1992, did you -- were you the coroner for the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. Not only 1992, but before the war too, and especially during the war, and I still do that to establish the natural death. During the war, of course, I was more engaged in this because our young doctors were -- had their duties on the battlefront and other doctors who were there were always on duty, so that I was one of those few who had enough time to perform this kind of duty which also falls under the health care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in June 1992, do you know if there was the Keraterm investigating centre in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that. I know of the investigating centre at Keraterm and I also know of the investigating centre at Omarska and also the collection centre in Omarska -- in Trnopolje, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, do you remember if in June 1992, you received an invitation from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I did. That was the only invitation and the -- my only visit to Keraterm throughout the war or, rather, before or after in my lifetime, because I've never been to Keraterm before or after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was the role of the investigating centre at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: The investigating centre at Keraterm, as far as I know, helped people who had transgressed laws, who had participated in the attack on Prijedor or in any other way cooperated, took part in the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when did this attack on Prijedor occur?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: It was in late May. I wouldn't know the exact date, 30th or 31st, but it was the very last days of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, and who is it that called you from Keraterm and how did he do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: That call came to my place, to my home, and it was Zivko Knezevic whom I knew well from before the war and about whom I know that he is a retired policeman. He called my place and said that a death had occurred in Keraterm and asked me to go there and establish the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he establish communication with you; how did he call you?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic called me by telephone, my home number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he did that and spoke to you, did he tell you why he was calling you?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that somebody had died and asked me to come and make record of this death of that person who was in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I believe I can. It was in the latter half of June and it was over the weekend, because on workdays, I was not at home, I worked. So it must have been either Saturday or Sunday. And now when I think back, in view of the duties that I had at the time, I usually did my shopping on Saturday mornings, and Sundays I spent at home preparing food for that day for my workdays, so I think that this call came on Sunday in the morning hours because Mr. Zivko Knezevic found me at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us if that was towards the end of the month or in the early part of the second half of the month?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: It was in the beginning of the second half of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then go to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I was about to explain why I'm so sure that it was the beginning of the latter half of June rather than the last week because the -- I spent the last week of June in Banja Luka as my daughter was about to deliver. I was to become a grandmother for the first time. So the last weekend in June I spent in Banja Luka, and the weekend before the last one, I was in Prijedor. So it must have been the first weekend in the second half of June. But I forgot the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you respond to Mr. Knezevic's call?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you go to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Mr. Zivko Knezevic called me by telephone, as I told you. I was at home and it was in the morning hours on Sunday, and he said that in a few minutes' time a car would arrive to fetch me, so that I went out of my apartment, went down, and indeed in a few minutes' time a green Mercedes pulled up, arrived there, and I remember it because it didn't happen all that often during the war, with a driver, and he took me to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us at what time did you arrive in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: It was in the morning, I think rather early, that is around 10.00 or half past or perhaps 11.00, because it was too early for lunch and it was a nice June morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Keraterm, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: As I entered the -- as I entered Keraterm, we passed by the guard booth and then I was taken to the rear part of the Keraterm, that is, to the end of the building which otherwise was a tile factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the car came to a stop, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: In the back part of the Keraterm yard, there were several young men in uniforms. There was Zivko Knezevic. And on the ground, on the concrete, there was a body of an adult, tall man, who -- well, it -- he didn't look any different from other bodies. That is, all I could see was that it was a body, a dead body, and that there were a few young, armed men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the position in which that body was lying?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, after all the time, it is very difficult to remember the details, but I think it was in supine position, on its back, on the concrete, in a pool of blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you find on the body?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, I first requested that the body be transferred to pallets, to wooden pallets which were in the immediate vicinity so as to perform an examination of that body superficially, and the present soldiers did that. That is, they moved the body to a wooden pallet in a corner right next to the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it your duty to establish if that person was dead?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. My duty was to establish the death, and according to my previous experience, my duty would be to remove the clothing from that body, to perform an examination of the body, external examination of the body, and to give my opinion as to the cause and time of death. However, Mr. Zivko Knezevic said that I should only establish that that person was dead, and when I requested that the clothes be removed from that body, Mr. Zivko said that there was no need for it and that all I had to do was to say whether the man was indeed dead, and what was -- what had been the cause of death, that is, whether it was violent or natural or -- and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, in view of your line of work, was it common to put -- to make a written finding on the site?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. I'm telling you, before or after that, what my experience told me, it was always to remove the clothes of the body, and they would always be held by persons present there, to perform an external examination of the body, and of course to write the finding which I would then type out later. But on this occasion, Zivko, Mr. Zivko, said that my duty there was merely to say whether that person was dead, and that he would write a memo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, did you know whose body that was?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Since I did not know of that man, that is, I could not identify the body, I asked Mr. Zivko Knezevic who that was and he said that it was a policeman from Ljubija. And I remembered his name because that surname is not all that common in Prijedor, and it was Drago Tokmadzic, a policeman from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, do you remember if you saw the death spots on the body?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Let me repeat, I must point it out again, the body was in a pool of blood, and on the face or rather exposed parts of the body, one could see very many haematoma, that is subcutaneous -- and I asked that the -- those present to move the body onto the pallet so as to examine the body. What I could see without removing the clothes was that the body -- that, first of all, the person did not show any signs of life. The man was evidently dead. But apart from the -- certain causes of death which showed that the death must have occurred at least two hours earlier and perhaps even much earlier than that, because, yes, there was rigor mortis was present there, pallor was present there, and the body was very cold. I did not see those spots because I did not take the clothes off the body -- off the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, as a physician, can you tell us how much -- after how much time do the death spots appear on a body after death has occurred? How long does it take for the death spots to appear?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: The death spots occur several hours later, between six and eight hours, but rigor mortis sets in two hours after death, which means that the maximum time that rigor mortis can set in after death is two hours. Rigor mortis lasts for 48 hours and disappears over the next 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether temperature and weather affects rigor mortis or, rather, the appearance of rigor mortis? Do climatic conditions and temperature affect that?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. It depends on the external temperature, the heat or the cold. It can set in a little late or rigor mortis can set in a little earlier, in the space of one hour, or if it's cold, in the space of two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, if you count the time that you arrived on the spot and count back, when could the death of Drago Tokmadzic have occurred? What would you say the time of death was?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: As I was there sometime after 10.00, death certainly occurred that night, perhaps towards dawn, as far as I was able to establish. I failed to mention that on the external parts of the body on clothing, there were no traces of firearms, but exclusively traces of blows with a blunt object, whether it was a leg, a kick or a rifle butt or a baton of any kind, a truncheon, I can't say. But with respect to the bruises and the large amount of blood found around the body, I can say with certainty that it was a violent death as a result of a blow with a blunt object in certain parts of the body. This led -- could have been a rupture of the liver that was caused by those blows or a brain haemorrhage. I wouldn't like to venture, to make a definite conclusion as to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were on the spot, do you happen to remember the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 behaviour of Zivko Knezevic, the man who had called you to come? How did he behave?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Mr. Zivko Knezevic was extremely angry, and I never remember seeing him that angry before. And with a very angry voice, he said to the people present, to the young people present -- I can't say whether they were policemen or soldiers, I don't remember what kind of uniforms they were wearing, but he did say with a very angry voice that he had expressly ordered that the prisoners should not be beaten. He was very angry and said why had that been done. The people who were present were silent, they bowed their heads, and accepted his criticism and made no comments of their own to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you had done your job, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I offered to write out a written report. I said to Zivko that I would do that because it was customary. I would jot it down on the spot, and then type it out at home, but Mr. Zivko said that there was no need for me to write down any finding, any conclusion, and that it was sufficient for him to make an official note and to take it to the public security station, or rather, the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question for you, Mrs. Andjelkovic, although I think you've answered it, but I'll repeat it nonetheless. Did you at any other time receive calls to go to the Keraterm investigation centre to establish the cause of death? Were you ever called out before?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No, neither to Keraterm or Omarska. That was the only time, the first, only, and last time that I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions for the witness for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Deretic. Dr. Andjelkovic, you will now be answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor, and I see that Mr. Saxon is on his feet. Mr. Saxon, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, when did you become a doctor; in what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So today you've been a doctor for 33 years. In 1992, you had been a doctor for 25 years; is that a fair calculation?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know somebody named Aleksandar Bereta?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Aleksandar Bereta politically active in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Dr. Aleksandar Bereta, up until that time, up until 1992, was my director. He was the director of the health institution that I worked in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is today, in 2001, is Dr. Aleksandar Bereta politically active in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I think he is because I've been seeing him on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I apologise for interrupting. Mr. President, I object to the question asked by the Prosecutor linked to the political activities of a third individual who was not mentioned here. I don't think that is in order or proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, perhaps you jumped the gun. I don't know where Mr. Saxon's question is leading to. Could you enlighten us, please, Mr. Saxon, as to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I am interested in exploring the political connections of this witness and her political ties which would, perhaps, be relevant to issues of bias and credibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, please proceed. Mr. Deretic, could you switch your microphone off, please. Mr. Saxon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me try to be briefer. Are you a member, today, of a political party?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No, I never was a member nor am I now, nor will I be ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, a man by the name of Ljuban Andzic testified before this Trial Chamber several months ago, and Mr. Andzic testified that, "The medical state in Omarska was catastrophic during in the summer of 1992 due to shortage of supplies, medication, and medical workers." How would you describe the health care situation in the town of Prijedor and the municipality of Prijedor overall during that time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, I remember the situation very well. I can't say anything about Omarska, because in Omarska was under the competency of the military medical service so my service did not comprise Omarska or Keraterm. But we were there in the Trnopolje collection centre, we were present all the time. As far as the health situation and the epidemiological situation, when it -- we're speaking of Prijedor during the war, I think that it is thanks to the previous preventive measures that had been undertaken to a maximum extent, that means to say vaccination against infectious diseases for the population, the fact that the water was hygienic and potable. Regular controls of the health of the population, regardless of all the upsetting and chaotic situation because of the enormous number of refugees, I think that I can say that the epidemiological situation in Prijedor was favourable. But I cannot say that for all the centres and households where there were a great number of refugees. It was summertime, with no electricity, no refrigerators, no possibility of coming by foodstuffs, but we did manage to survive. And as I say, the epidemiological situation was in order. That is to say no -- none of the typical infectious diseases that could arise in situations of this kind occurred, like jaundice, dysentery, and so on, so forth. We managed to avoid all those diseases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, what were your professional duties and responsibilities between May of 1992 and May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: The same as they are today. That is to say, to follow the health situation of the population, to have a registrar of all those suffering from infectious diseases, malignant diseases, diabetes, leukaemia, keep records, medical records of that kind, and many other illnesses too, and to establish control over the water supply, the sewage system, vaccinations, to carry vaccinations out, and all the other things that my regular job comprises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those wartime conditions, were you very busy during that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes, of course I was, because we had a large number of refugees, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the -- it was your duty to follow the health situation of the population. Would that include the people who were being detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No. I have already said that under my competences was only the collection centre in Trnopolje, which is where the civilian individuals, the detainees were. And Omarska and Keraterm were other establishments, that is to say, under civilian competence, Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that as an epidemiologist with 25 years' experience, in 1992 you never inquired or investigated as to the health conditions of the population detained in the Omarska camp? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I think that at this point in time, it is not our topic, but let me say that at the time I was informed that it was the health service of the army that was in charge of that, that the military epidemiologist was in charge of monitoring the health situation of the detainees in those investigation centres. That was under military jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the director -- your director or supervisor in 1992 was Aleksandar Bereta. Was he a member of the SDS in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have an official position in the SDS in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, I really can't say. All I know is that he performed the functions of director. That is to say, he was head of the institution I worked in. And I had so many problems myself at work, at home, I didn't have any time to wonder whether somebody was a politician or things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that on one occasion in June of 1992, you went to the -- you went to the Keraterm camp. How did the Keraterm camp smell?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Quite obviously there was no special smell because I didn't -- don't remember it being special in any way, entering into the -- I went into the courtyard of Keraterm. I didn't go into the buildings. I was in the courtyard and the courtyard is a big one, it is wide and long, and had there been an intensive smell of any kind, such as ammoniac from the toilets or anything of that kind, it would have reached my nose. But as I say, I didn't notice any specific smell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the prisoners look that day you went there?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I did not see a single detainee. It was a courtyard, a long building with several metal doors, and all the doors were closed, as far as I remember. At the entrance gate, I saw several guards. I can't say with certainty whether there were two or three. And I saw a couple of those young, armed men around the body. There was nobody else in the courtyard apart from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Keraterm camp was within a kilometre or two of the centre of Prijedor town; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. It was at the exit, as you go out of the centre of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, Doctor, that during the summer of 1992, even on the day that you arrived in that camp, that there were at a minimum hundreds of men detained at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I probably knew because it was rumoured in town, but they were rumours so I didn't have any proper information. And as I say, I went about doing my own job and looking after my family, so I can't really give you any real information. It would just be hearsay on the basis of rumours that I had heard in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as an epidemiologist with many years of experience, did you even bother to inquire about the health and hygienic conditions of all these people who were being detained in this factory, Keraterm, within a kilometre or two of the centre of Prijedor during the summer of 1992? Did you even bother to inquire?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I didn't make any special inquiries, I must say, because I thought that it was under the authority of another institution. But I did have information, for example, about Omarska, that they had quite a lot of diarrhea, both the detainees and the guards and all the people working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned that when you arrived at Keraterm that morning to examine the body, although you offered to write a report, Zivko Knezevic told you that there was no need for you to do that, that merely he would write a memo. Isn't it standard procedure for a physician who examines a body and declares that a person is dead to write an official report about the body that they have examined and the death?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. It is the duty of the person examining the body externally, and all the examinations I did, and when I followed up on them, on the spot, I would jot down my findings, and then at home or at work I would type out my report on a typewriter in addition to this official report given to the official individual that called me to establish the cause and time of death, I would write a certificate for the family in order for them to be able to bury the individual according to the religious rites, depending on the faith the individual belongs to. But for Drago Tokmadzic, Mr. Zivko said that there was no need for me to do that, that he would write his own official note. And nobody, no family member, came to ask for a certificate that we generally -- always hand out when the cause of death is either natural or violent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to talk to you about that. Did you know the person -- did you know the person who was lying there dead? Was that someone you knew?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never -- were you shown any identification for that person?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to any family members or friends of that person?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No. As I said, no family member appeared to ask any information, nobody turned up of the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Doctor, that the body that you examined that morning at Keraterm was actually the body of another physician, a man named Dr. Zeljko Sikura a Croat who had been killed in Keraterm that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were --

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: My colleague Sikura, I know him very well, and there was absolutely no chance that that was him, no chance at all, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What steps did you take -- well let me back up a bit. A man by the name of Vasif Gutic testified at this trial about the terrible hygienic conditions in which the persons detained at the Trnopolje camp lived, and the serious medical and psychological problems suffered by many of the detainees at Trnopolje. What steps did you take to alleviate those bad conditions?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: There was some technical interference so I didn't understand what you asked me, but I think I grasped your question. I think in that Trnopolje, everything was done that could have been in order to ensure normal conditions under such abnormal circumstances, that is to say, to ensure that the water was hygienic that was brought in with systems, to ensure enough toilets and enough food, which the Red Cross supplied. I asked for tea for the detainees so that those who were having stomach troubles could drink tea. The children played in the Trnopolje club, and in the halls. The pupil -- the classrooms were full. As I say, the conditions were wartime conditions, abnormal conditions and shocking for me, but not that there was danger of any kind. We tried to provide -- we had associates, Muslims and Serbs, that helped me in administering the hygienic measures as far as possible in the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the Trnopolje camp or collection centre finally vacated?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I really can't remember the date. I have it jotted down somewhere in my notebooks, but I can't tell you now. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you that the Trnopolje camp was finally vacated of the last of its detainees around the beginning of December 1992, would that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I know that after the last people from the collection centre left, I came to see what kind of clearing up of the terrain, how the terrain could be cleared and cleansed to ensure that the school can be used for the purposes for which it was intended, and the premises were intended before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could place on the ELMO, and if the registrar's assistant in Banja Luka could show the witness a copy of Exhibit 3/253. Dr. Andjelkovic -- and by the way, Your Honours, this is a document from the Prijedor collection. We have provided to the registry a declaration from Mr. Mazhar Inayat from the Prosecution's office, explaining how this document came into our possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you see in front of you the copy, the version in your own language, please, that begins with the word "conclusion" in the text? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes, but this is the first time that I see this conclusion and that I am looking at a conclusion at this document and decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just going to ask you to comment about it. This Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 document is dated the 25th of December 1992. It is entitled Conclusion. It is signed by Dr. Milan Kovacevic as chairman of the executive committee. Sentence one says, "To accept the offer submitted by 4 Juli (public service enterprise) in Prijedor for cleaning up the grounds around Trnopolje primary school for 4.031.500 dinars." Sentence two says, "To appoint Dr. Dusanka Andjelkovic as the supervisory organ overseeing the cleaning up operation." Do you see what I've just read out loud, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I see it, and I'm holding it in my hands, and I'm reading this for the first time in my life. This is the first time that I am looking at this. To tell you the truth, the supervising of the cleaning up of the operation I did because I considered it to be my duty, and not response to a conclusion that I knew nothing about. And I know nothing about it now. This is the first time that I'm seeing it. So together with the sanitary inspection, I worked together with the sanitary inspection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you considered it your duty to oversee the clean-up of the -- of what had been the Trnopolje camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not consider it your duty to even inquire about the health and hygiene conditions at the Keraterm camp or at the Omarska camp; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Let me repeat my answer once again. It was the health service of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, just a moment please. I think that this is the third time that you are asking the same question, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it the truth, Doctor, that more than just cleaning up the area of the camp in Trnopolje was required? That it was important also to destroy evidence of wrongdoing at the Trnopolje centre, such as blood?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Sir, I guarantee that, apart from the dirt and the old clothes scattered around, old stoves, old fridges and many other refuse of that kind, I saw nothing else neither was I in charge of anything else. I didn't see any blood during my work in the collection centre or after I went. I can swear to that, and I speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth when I say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your director, the director or your supervisor in 1992, Mr. Bereta, he eventually became the president of the SDS in Prijedor; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I really can't remember the -- all the political parties and all that. As I told you, I had a lot of family problems. I had a lot of -- my husband had serious health problems. I had problems with the population. So I didn't delve in politics. I wasn't interested. I had to contend with everything that happened to me during years which should have been the best years of my life, if can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were able to remember the name of Drago Tokmadzic; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the name, and I am saying so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. I should also like to benefit from -- to benefit from this occasion. On page 14, for the third time rather than the first time, as it says there. Mr. Deretic, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, a number of them. They are all very short, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, at the beginning of your testimony, you spoke about when you had been called to Keraterm, and you said that it was the second weekend in the latter half of the month -- no, sorry, the first weekend. Could you be more specific and tell us when is it that you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, you know, when I take the film back, and when I go through all that I've already explained to you, it was on the 21st of June - because I looked up the dates in the calendar - in the morning hours. So it could have been 10.00 or 11.00. It was Sunday. It was before noon. But not the last Sunday, I am absolutely sure about that. So it could have been one before last Sunday in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, do you know Dr. Sikura?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes, very well indeed, because we worked together. He worked for the same establishment as I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his first name?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: His first name was Mladen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please -- my learned friend asked you in view -- in the light of your profession, why didn't you do more in relation to other investigation centres, that is Omarska and Trnopolje? Had you wanted to, would you have been allowed? Would you have been able to enter those investigation -- that is, collection centres, in view of the time when all this was going on?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I admit that I wouldn't have, neither I nor my associates, because I never work alone, I always take along a team of technicians or physicians with me. And Trnopolje was my duty, the municipality was my duty, and about this, nobody had notified me, nobody asked for me, and I do not think they would have admitted me into the compound of those investigating centres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more question. On the document that was just shown you, I'm referring to the conclusion, and I'm talking about the document in Serbian language, is there a signature beneath the typed-out name of late Dr. Milan Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No. It says the chairman of the executive committee, Dr. Milan Kovacevic, sui mano, there is no signature, and there is Ostojic a lawyer, with a signature, but I was never issued that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. The Defence has no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Mr. Deretic. Judge Riad? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like to have two clarifications to help me understand what you said. Concerning your visit to testify about the death of Drago Tokmadzic, you mentioned that you usually would write findings and conclusion, and also for the family of the deceased, you would have to give them a document to bury the deceased, and that Mr. Knezevic told you that there was no need to write any finding or conclusion. What did you write?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: In that particular case, nothing, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you write it was a natural death or there was no death? What did you write? Nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: As I said, nothing at all. I did not write anything at all, but I informed Mr. Knezevic verbally that the cause of death was violent and it was due to blows with a blunt object all over the body, and that the death had occurred a number of hours before the examination, and he said that he would write -- yes, yes, what he said was the official note, and that is the term that is normally used in medicine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And in these camps, they usually wrote their official notes and nobody -- you were not asked to come, or any of your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I believe I said that already, it was my first and last time that I went to the camp, and I am not aware of any other deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Are you aware that other people of your colleagues or subordinates were called? Or did you see any reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No, no. I did not see any such thing or talk about this, because my job was completely different, and it just happened so because there were no younger men to do that. It would have been much more logical rather than a woman of an advanced age to go and do this. So it was just by accident, by chance, that they called me to go and do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you can understand -- you can answer me if I ask you what urged them to ask you specially concerning this Drago Tokmadzic death and not any other death? Why was this particularly important to call, as you said, a person of your status? Since they didn't want you to make any report or anything, why did they call you?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, yes, I also thought about it, and decided that it must have been acquaintanceship of long standing with Mr. Zivko Knezevic, who was a retired policeman and with whom I cooperated closely in time of communism, but he was reactivated at that time, and he was the chief of police in a part of Prijedor, and that is the part of Prijedor where Keraterm was, so I suppose he simply remembered me and called me, and I suppose he called me because it was a policeman's body, that is his colleague's body. That is what I thought, but it was -- it wasn't an official view, an official stand that would have been presented to me at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in fact you did not go in your official capacity, and you said it was the only time you went and you think it was not in your official capacity or to make a report? Sorry, I have no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No English translation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English on this microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could repeat that question. Judge Fouad Riad, would you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll read it from the transcript. I said, so you did not go in your official capacity, and that you said it was the only time you went and you think it was not in your official capacity to make a report? No answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that -- I cannot see the witness on the monitor. I don't know. Witness, can you hear me? Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It appears that the call has been disconnected. So I will check and see how long it will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic? Did you manage to establish the connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I cannot, but I believe this is a convenient time to indicate -- or rather, after the question on page 25, line 4, the witness said something completely different from what is in the transcript. So perhaps after we establish the connection, perhaps I shall go back to that, although I will let you know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall then wait. Madam Registrar, where are we? Do you think that the connection will be established? I see that it has been established. So Judge Riad, will you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. I can see it in the transcript. You said you did not go in your official capacity and that you don't know or you do not think that other of your subordinates or colleagues went and you were not asked to make a report. Is that a fair conclusion of what you said?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, more or less. I mean every time when a physician is called to certify death, he goes. Then the team involves the criminal investigation inspector, a judge of the district court, and a physician, a medical practitioner. And on that occasion, there were only the chief police of that part of the Prijedor municipality and myself, that is, there was no judge, there was no criminal investigation inspector and there was no request to write out the finding, the official note, and the official opinion, as is customary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was not an official visit?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say whether it was official or not. To my mind, it was official because things like that do not happen every day. And it is not without any significance for a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, then Mr. Knezevic told you that he would write his own report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, and very much so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he wanted you to come to make it possible for him to write a report?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And do you know what he has put in his report?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And was this a regular procedure?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. My other question concerns this, I think, decision which appointed you as the supervisory organ overseeing the clean-up operation which has been read to you. You said that you didn't know about it, but you still considered it would be your duty to do it. Why would it be your duty to do it?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Well, that falls within the jurisdiction of the municipal epidemiologist and after all emergency situation, there is a rule that something that was disrupted has to be brought back to a normal situation. That even in a case of a funeral or something, and especially following the situation in these collection centres when there was a great deal of garbage, of excrement, and everything else which had to be cleaned up so that the elementary school, and that was an elementary school for children from the neighbouring area, the school had simply to be put back in its normal state so the children could resume attending their classes there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it fell within your profession or your competence that -- which you mentioned was the hygienic -- to protect the hygienic conditions of the population, you think it was threatening the hygienic conditions of the population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes. You put it quite well. That is the proper answer to that question except that I was a physician and therefore, I was -- I served as a consultant, as an advisor, and the municipal public services issue the order in writing what needs to be done so as to implement all the measures that were requisite at that place. And I am merely an advisory body, but the order is issued by a municipal official, that is, the sanitation inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic, did Mr. Knezevic, when he called you to come to Keraterm, did he tell you why he was calling you? You've told us why you think he may have called you, but did he tell you why he was calling on you, even though it was out of your competence, your normal jurisdictional competence, or did you ask him at that time why he was calling on you?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I did not ask him that because I thought that because it was Sunday, Sunday morning, he simply had failed to find any of other physicians in the town, and that must have been the reason apart from the fact that we were good friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But it never happened again. You were never called by him or by anyone else to go to Keraterm or Omarska. You've told us that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: That is right. Never again. Nobody called me either before that or after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you, in late July of 1992, hear by word of mouth or otherwise about a large number of deaths that occurred on the night of July 24th, early morning of 25th in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we -- it has been disconnected. We now have to wait. I believe it's been re-established now. I do not know whether the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 witness can answer Judge Wald's question or does the question need to be repeated? I believe that the connection has been re-established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, it's a short one, Doctor, and that is: Did you hear by word of mouth or otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Judge Wald, but we do not have the connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you see we are about to finish the examination of this witness. I am being told that we have problems with the connection because of the weather in Banja Luka, and this, of course, causes problems, difficulties with communication. I must ask the parties to try to make the best of the time today, because it appears that we shall have problems, but we are waiting for the connection so as to finish with this witness before the break. Oh, yes, the connection has been established. Yes, Judge Wald?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Doctor, did you hear about a large number of deaths that occurred in one night, around July 24th to 25th, 1992, in Keraterm? Did you hear about them?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I cannot pinpoint the date when the rumour started but, yes, there were some rumours going about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. But nobody, to your knowledge, neither you nor anybody in your health centre, was called at that time to Keraterm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: It is. I am not aware of that. I do not know if somebody else went, but the health centre is very large, it has 350 people on its staff, so one cannot really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Moving on to Trnopolje, which was within your competence, when a death occurred at the camp in Trnopolje, were you or someone from your centre and the regular investigative team that you told us about, were they called down to register and make an official report on those deaths in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: It -- in all likelihood, but I do not know of any such case of any deaths, or that I personally was not present at any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, two last questions. One, even though you have told us that you did not attend any deaths other than the one you mentioned, or testified about here, in Keraterm or Omarska because that was not in the competence of the civilian authorities, as an epidemiologist and as somebody interested in public health, was there any communication from the military authorities who were running those camps, Omarska and Keraterm, when deaths occurred? For instance, if there was an outbreak of diarrhea, which you mentioned, in Omarska, or if somebody died in Omarska or Keraterm, were you in the public-health sector of Prijedor informed about that? Was there any communication about how many deaths were occurring in the other camps so that you could keep track of any epidemic problems?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I did not receive any such information because the military have their own vertical chain of information which they used to inform the relevant institutions, and these investigating centres were separated from the civilian population. That is, there was no danger of any epidemic spreading outside those investigating centres. So I presume it was for that reason why they did not notify me, either about the epidemiological situation or about deaths in those investigating centres to which I did not go, being a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How do you think that could be, Doctor? Because you had guards and interrogators coming every day back and forth, and you also had some portion of the detainees being released on some occasions back into the normal populace. I'm just wondering if it didn't occur as a problem to at least keep in some communication, there were several thousand people being detained in Keraterm and Omarska and there was interchange with the regular population.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I'm really not in a position to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Because I was not kept abreast insofar as guards or detainees were concerned or anything. I was performing civilian duty in an exceptionally difficult situation in a municipality where there were migrations, shortages of power supply, shortages of water supply. Huge problems existed there so that this other kind of problems were not mine. At least, that is how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. My last question. Do you know whether or not similar cleanup operations occurred in Keraterm -- after Keraterm and Omarska were closed as occurred when Trnopolje was closed? I understand you were not responsible but I just wonder whether or not you know whether any of those sites of the other two camps underwent similar cleaning, cleanup operations, to the one you supervised in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Again, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Deretic, you had a question which you raised, I believe. If I understood you well, you told us that you wanted to ask -- that you had asked a question and it was not properly interpreted. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Page 25, line 4, the transcript says in relation to the official note mentioned by the witness, and the transcript said "that which is in use in medicine on a regular basis." And Dr. Andjelkovic said that it was not a normal procedure to mention the official note as -- that it was not a medical term. So that is my objection, and I'd like merely to clarify this and would ask the witness to help us. Very short question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the problem is that we have lost the witness again but we shall come back to it. Yes, I suppose you will have to ask the question again and not make any explanations because the -- when the question is repeated, one does not know whether the witness will repeat the same answer. We always have this question. There are these allegations and we do not get the same answer, but we have to wait for the witness to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting, but I will take advantage of this brief break to say that Mr. Radic is not feeling well, so may I have the court's permission for Mr. Radic to be taken out of the courtroom? He has a very bad headache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic, for bringing that to our attention, but I think that we are going to take a break and then you will be able to -- yes, well, I think that Mr. Radic can be given permission to leave, if the security service agrees, if it has the means to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the witness back again. Witness, we have no other questions to ask you. We thank you for having come, and as I say, we have no further questions for you today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Mr. Deretic, please go ahead with your question. I apologise, Witness. We have one more question for you. We've lost the communication again. Go ahead quickly. Further examined by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me, Dr. Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The official note, is that a normal term used in medicine that you spoke about a moment ago, the official note?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA Andjelkovic
utterances.text: An official note is never used as a term in medical practice and that is why I remembered it because I never used that term, and may I make another -- put something right. It was Sikura Zeljko, not Mladen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Prosecutor have any questions, any response from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Dr. Andjelkovic, we really have come to the end of your testimony. We thank you very much, and wish you every success back at your work, thank you. Let us take a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time, the Prosecution would like to move for the admission of Exhibit 3/253 which was shown to the prior witness; however, just for clarification, I would make this offer with one caveat. Mr. Deretic correctly pointed out that there is apparently a mistake in the English translation in that underneath the name of Dr. Milan Kovacevic, we see in brackets the word "signed." However, on the original B/C/S version, there appears to be no such signature. So the Prosecution would inform the Court that we will resubmit this document for -- to the translation unit one more time to make sure that we have an accurate translation, or if it needs to be corrected, and then we will submit a revised version which could be given a bis number, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence of Mr. Zigic is absolutely opposed to having a document of this kind tendered into evidence, admitted into evidence for a number of reasons. The first reason being that we were not presented with the original document. The second reason is that it was not signed by one of the individuals who, in fact, made the conclusion, as alleged by the Prosecution, made the conclusion. And thirdly and most importantly, the witness we examined said that to the present day, she had never seen this document nor does she have any knowledge about the document regardless of the fact that it has the name of the witness we heard testimony from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, would you like to respond quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, I will try to respond, I think, in the reverse order. Although the witness said that she had never seen this document before, this document bears her name. It bears the indication that she is a physician. It reflects her performing a certain function which she acknowledged during her testimony that she performed, in fact, she acknowledged that she had a duty to perform it. So the Prosecution would submit that it is directly relevant to the testimony of this witness although Mr. Deretic is correct that apparently on the B/C/S there is no signature by Dr. Milan Kovacevic, there is clearly a signature underneath the name of the secretary of the executive committee, Mr. Zdravko Ostojic, and that is clearly, at a minimum, more than an indicia of authenticity which is the standard of admission of hearsay evidence in this Tribunal. With regard to the original of this document, I cannot guarantee that what the Prosecution seized was an original copy, although if I had to make a guess -- excuse me, I cannot guarantee that the Prosecution seized the original document itself as opposed to a photocopy. I think it is very possible that what was seized was a photocopy, which is why we are presenting a photocopy in court. We do have a declaration from Mr. Mazhar Inayat as to how this document was seized. He does not specify in his declaration whether this document was seized in its original form or simply as a photocopy of the original. But in any event, I think that is certainly enough for the Trial Chamber's purposes, at least for the admission of this document, and then later on, obviously at the end of the case, the Trial Chamber can make up its mind as to what weight to give to this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I just add one more sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a witness -- we had a witness. The Prosecution put its point forward. You put your point forward. We are going to end the debate there and the judges shall confer for a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has decided to admit the document, and afterwards, it will see what weight it will attach to it, with the reservation that you will, of course, correct the translation. What number, Madam Registrar, do we have for the document? Is it 3/253?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once you have established the translation of the document, we shall admit it into evidence. Mr. Deretic, the next witness is Dragomir Saponja -- no? Jugoslav Gnjatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. The next witness is Jugoslav Gnjatovic. Unfortunately, I have to inform the Chamber that upon my arrival in Prijedor on Friday, I was not able to contact Mr. Saponja. And unfortunately, he is not in Prijedor. In view of the fact that his parents informed me that he was travelling, I can tell you that he will not be testifying either today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness that we are now going to hear, Mr. Deretic, is it Jugoslav Gnjatovic? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am going to address the witness. Witness, I see you're there. Thank you for coming. Would you please stand and read the solemn declaration which Ms. Melinda is going to hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Thank you for coming. You will start off by answering questions put to you by Mr. Deretic. Mr. Deretic, your witness. Examined by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Dusan Jugoslav Gnjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm afraid I can't hear the witness's answers. Perhaps there is a technical fault. I can't hear what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we are having a problem with the channels. Now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Gnjatovic?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when you were born and where.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of March, 1958 in Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you reside at present?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor, Partizanska Street, number 69.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity and religion?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb of the orthodox faith. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, after the war broke out in the area of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you mobilised into the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was? What date?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: It was between the 3rd and 4th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were mobilised, where were you deployed?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I was deployed down there, the Stadion OFK Berek that was the outskirts of Prijedor. Berek. That was the point we were assigned to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the OFK you mentioned mean?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: It was the youth football club. "OFK" is the abbreviation for youth football club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days did you spend at that location?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 7th of June, 7th or 8th, three or four days, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were on duty at that point --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I was saying while you were on duty there, did you find any moped or motorcycle there?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, an automatic one in a shed by a Muslim house. They are all Muslim houses round about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use it?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go riding that moped?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I went three and a half kilometres outside Prijedor, to my aunt Milka, at a place called Gomjenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at your aunt's?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: An hour or two, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did you go back to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Nearby, there was a restaurant called Stari Hrast, and I was stopped there by four military policemen, and among them was Zoka Tomic and he said -- he asked me, "Why did you wound me in the leg?" Probably when the attack took place, he had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What attack are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: The attack on Prijedor, when that took place. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the date of the attack, when it took place?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was between the 31st and the 1st, between May and June, the 31st of May. The night between the 31st of May and the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were stopped by those policemen, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they took away my motorcycle and put me in a car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: They took me off to Keraterm because the collection centre already existed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you got out of the car, were you physically abused?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Zoran Tomic hit me with his pistol in the -- in my right eye and I suffered a serious injury to my right eye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a scar after that occurrence?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have got one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the investigation centre of Keraterm, do you know whether people who had taken part in the attack on Prijedor had already been detained there?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the people who were non-Serbs, that is to say, the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why had they been detained?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, principally because of the attack and people they had found weapons on and thought -- had suspected that they had taken part in the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Keraterm, was there a room with Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they also locked up, detained?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because they stole, they stole cars, things of that kind. Mostly because of theft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, how long were you in that improvised military prison?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were held in a room there two to three days and then were transferred to the other side of the military police building. The other side was where the military police was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the other side," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean the other side of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the Keraterm building?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the side of the building where we were held for two or three days, there were Muslims and Croats there, and on the opposite side of the Keraterm, there was the military police, behind that building, behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your status in that military prison?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was normal, but we weren't allowed to move around. We had the status of military policemen, we had our meals together, but we didn't have our weapons, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to move around in front of the rooms that you were put up in?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go on towards the front side of Keraterm where the other people were detained who had taken part in the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, we weren't allowed to go there. It was forbidden. All movement there was forbidden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, did you know Zoran Zigic?
