utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew him -- I've known him for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any family relations, were you connected by family?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of family ties?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were married to two sisters. We each married a sister, but we were -- we were both separated from the two sisters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean that they were your first wives, wives from your first marriage?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your relationships were with Zoran Zigic up until 1993 when he was detained, taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- how can I put it? We weren't actually too -- there was a certain distance between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you contact -- have contacts, did you see each other?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, if we would happen to meet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you friends? Did you socialise?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, yes. While he was a taxi driver, I would happen to drop by because I lived nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were detained in Keraterm by the military police, did you happen to see Zoran Zigic at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he would come by because there were ten soldiers that were detained there, ten of us soldiers, and he would come by from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why Zoran came?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he would bring some cigarettes, sometimes some alcoholic beverage, that kind of thing, because there was a general crisis and cigarettes were hard to come by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when Zoran would come by, what was his behaviour like?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the entrance where the guard was, we would hear him coming 50 or 60 metres away. You would know that Zoran was there immediately because he had a loud voice. I don't know how to explain it. He had a loud voice and you could always hear him when he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him for the first time in Keraterm, was he injured at all?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The hand of his right arm was bandaged -- of his left arm was bandaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he came, did he complain of suffering pain?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He kept his hand raised up by his chin and he had to drink some -- take some pills. He complained a great deal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Zigic Zoran was doing in the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: What I learnt from the other detained military policemen, he brought bread in a van and would also come on an automatic motorcycle. But he would come by because he knew all the guys that were detained there. He knew them from town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he contact you, I mean the people that were detained?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he would come and chat to us. He would sit around with us even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he know the military policemen who took care of you?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he contact -- have contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He chatted to them just like he chatted to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember during that period of time how many times you saw Zoran Zigic, how many days? Was it days, month, a longer, a shorter period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, he would come by five or six times, perhaps seven times. A number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran Zigic under the influence of alcohol when he dropped by to see you?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could smell it too. You could smell alcohol on his breath, and he was different when he had had a drink. I've known him for many years and he was different. His behaviour was different. He became more aggressive when he drank. And also because of his hand -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he would come by, would you hear Zigic first before you actually saw him?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would hear him at the entrance, at the gate. He would be shouting, and I would hear him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he shouting at?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Usually the person on duty at the gate, a guard or somebody from the police. It wasn't important, but he always wanted to be -- I don't know how to explain this -- he always --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they having an argument of any kind when he raised his voice and shouted or did he joke around with people?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. Mostly it was a joke, and then if you listened to that, you might think that he was having an argument with someone but he was actually joking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, did you know a man by the name of Emsud Bahonjic in those days?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn anything about that particular individual while you were detained by the military police?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did hear that people referred to him as the Singapurac because he was arrested with a Singapurka rifle, which is the deadliest rifle. That's what I heard from the policemen, that they had detained him, the other side. Who brought him in, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the man?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, but when he was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the policeman that took us there -- the toilets were blocked up so we had to go to the toilet over there, and Edgun [phoen] said, "Look at this Singapurac, the one they arrested. He's lying down dead on the pallets." And I went up and saw the body. I didn't know him myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you happen to notice the position he was lying in, the individual that that person claimed was?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was lying down on the pallets, the wooden pallets, on his back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember which of the military policemen mentioned that name to you or pointed out the body to you?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: It was Zoran Marijanovic. He was a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go up to the body?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything on the body?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could see he had a lot of blue bruises, black bruises, probably from blows with a blunt object, on his head, his chest, his arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you happen to hear about the cause of death, what caused his death?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: From beatings, that's what they said, that they beat him regularly, non-stop. Now, who beat him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from those men with whom you were there, or military policemen, that Zoran Zigic took part in beating that man?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. That's a leading question. Mr. Deretic is leading the witness with regard to this aspect because the witness said he didn't know, he didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I did not hear the interpretation at all. I apologise, Mr. President, I did not get the interpretation, so could my learned friend repeat his objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness said that he did not see or know about the beatings, but he said, as he observed injuries, that it was due to beatings. That's all. But Mr. Deretic's question was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. My question was very direct, but heeding to my colleague's objection, I asked very concretely and directly had the witness ever heard, because he never saw that, but had he ever heard about Zoran Zigic beating that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. According to the witness, he said that he was only shown the body and that nothing was said by the police officer or the soldier who took him there, so Mr. Deretic's subsequently -- his question was leading the witness to see as to whether Zoran Zigic was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps he meant somebody else except that policeman. Isn't that, Mr. Deretic? Had he heard something about it, apart, aside from that military policeman, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, can you please pinpoint the time when you saw that person about whom you had heard that his name was Emsud Bahonjic and when you saw his body on that pallet?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think about -- I cannot really say to a day but it must have been between the 16th or the 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there since the 8th of June and he must have been brought in on the 10th or 11th, or the 9th perhaps, I wouldn't know exactly. I heard about that, I did not see him, I just heard him being beaten, so it must have been about --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when were you released from the military prison?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Monday, the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Drago Tokmadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, did you know that person?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I did, for about 20 years. He was a policeman. He worked for the police station in Prijedor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did he come from? Where was he born?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Ljeskare, it's towards Donja Ljubija, down there. It's a place near Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Ljeskare a village bordering on Donja Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, a village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his wife?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I did; Mira.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did she work?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: She worked in the mine canteen, in the Ljubija mine. She was a cook there. She worked in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Drago Tokmadzic ever take you in or did he report you for a misdemeanour?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did have a couple of problems with him because of these reports, and on a couple of occasions his wife helped me. I asked her to do it so that he doesn't report, and they were good people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you see Drago Tokmadzic in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the same time, near those sand heaps. He was lying on the pallets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you specify the time when that happened?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I could. I left on Monday and on Sunday I saw him around 3.00 or half past in the afternoon but he was brought there before, but he must have been on the other side and beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at what stage was Drago Tokmadzic in when you saw him and in what position?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: He was also on the pallets, lying on his back. His head was bloody and he was all covered in bruises, black and blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he like as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: He was very strict. And according to stories -- I mean, I was on good terms with him, I didn't have any conflicts, but there were some people who held a grudge against me before the war so that may -- some people may have had a grudge against him, so perhaps that had a role in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly around the railway station. He was a very strict and dangerous policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you saw Drago Tokmadzic, did you speak with military policemen and other detainees about who had beaten him?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Why, no. I heard that he had been detained, but who beat him on that other side, I don't know, and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within that context, did you ever hear the name of Zoran Zigic mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who arrested and brought Drago Tokmadzic to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: According to the stories that I heard, it was Milan Curguz who did that, and he was a reserve policeman from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question: Can you tell us what you think of Zoran Zigic before the war and during that time, during the war before his detention.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come, what can I say because there is, after all, a drastic difference. How shall I explain it, because I've known him for ages and we were married to those two sisters. When he was sober, he was all right, but the moment he'd have one too many, he would become intolerable. I mean you couldn't talk to him. You couldn't find common language with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did he drink more, before or during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I think he drank a little bit more during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Deretic. Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were mobilised on the 3rd of June 1992; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. The 3rd, between the 3rd and the 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska, the so-called 5th Battalion, the town battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander when you were attached to the stadium, the Berek football stadium?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the commander was -- yeah, Krstan Josic was the commander of the town defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given a uniform and a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did get them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your assignment was to guard the entrance to the Berek stadium; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sure, and another part too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, did you know a person by the name of Dragoljub Lajic?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Dragoljub Lajic, you mean? Yes, I knew him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was also attached to the same unit; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Yes. Yes, but he was there a day or two and they let him go immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gnjatovic, you said that you took charge of a bicycle which was in a house, a Muslim house. Was it given to you or did you go into the house and take the bike away?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right. I took it myself, because all those houses were wide open and there was hardly a living soul there so that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct if I told you that you stole the bike from that house?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, well, if one says that I alleviated it, it means that I stole it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gnjatovic, were you prosecuted for any other offence before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the offences that you were charged with?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Theft mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were a convicted person before you were mobilised; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I was sentenced before the war. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long? What was the sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I spent twice, two years in the penitentiary in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gnjatovic, were you also charged with assault?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Against Prijedor? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, were you convicted of committing assault?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. Theft was the only thing. Oh, during the war, I was -- yes, I was convicted because of an assault, but that was in 1993 when I received two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will come to that later. Were you ever convicted before the war of committing assault or mischief in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for petty thefts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand what I am saying? I'm not talking about the thefts that you have said already that you have been convicted and been sentenced twice for you two years rigorous imprisonment sentences. I am talking about any assault charges that were brought against you. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were petty offences because I had got into a fight or something. Otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you convicted --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you convicted? Were you charged in a court of law for assault?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't -- it was mostly -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we'll move on. Mr. Gnjatovic, you said a person by the name of Tomicic confronted you in Prijedor when you took the bike, when you were riding the bike from your aunt's place to the town of Prijedor. Did he tell you as to why he took you to Keraterm or as to what offence you have committed?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it turned out that at the time of the attack on Prijedor that I supposedly wounded him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you deny that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you get my meaning? Impossible. Because between the 26th of May and the 3rd in the afternoon, I was in Omarska or, rather, they let us go and there were 2 Serbs and 20 Muslims. I was detained in Omarska like all the other Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I getting you correct, were you detained at Keraterm or was it in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of May until the 3rd of June, I was in Omarska. And between the 3rd and the 4th, I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your direct examination, you said that you were taken to Keraterm. Now, you say in cross-examination to my last question that you were in Omarska from the 26th of May until the 3rd of June. What is correct? Could you please explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Listen, I was mobilised on the 3rd, between the 3rd and the 4th. I was mobilised for the army. I was at the checkpoint until the night between the 7th and 8th and then I took this motorbike, and I went to my aunt and then I was taken -- then I was arrested and taken to Keraterm. I hardly spent three or -- four or five days as a mobilised man. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand it quite well now. Witness, how many days did you spend in Keraterm, in the room with the other soldiers, after you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Fourteen, maybe 15 days. If it's the 7th to the 22nd, how many days is it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did they question you or interrogate you while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who questioned you or interrogated?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were those in the military police. They were something like investigators. I can't really remember. How am I to explain it? They examined me like in that other separate room, but I could hear it from the other side of the wall how they examined Muslims. It was the also the police. They asked me who am I, what am I. They knew I had been released from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mention again Omarska. Could you explain whether -- tell the Chamber as to whether you were detained in Omarska or at any time you spent any time in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I spent in Omarska eight days. I was arrested and kept there with captured Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you kept or taken to Omarska, detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, I think we are going in circles here because something is wrong here. The witness has already said that he had been in Omarska between the 26th of May and the 3rd of June. So will you please move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested down in Puharska because -- because I stole a kitchen stove from a house. You know, whoever -- who -- it was only later that they said that I had taken part in the attack on Prijedor, that I had asked for somebody to be liquidated, but thank God -- I mean, I didn't do it but some people had a grudge against me. It's hot in here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it your position that you were detained in Omarska because you stole a stove from a Muslim dwelling?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what they say, and then between the 6th and the 27th of May, 1992, 13 buses left for Omarska then and I was in them. Nobody wanted to listen to you. There were friends of mine there but nobody wanted to talk to you even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, who was -- who were the personnel who was in Omarska when you were taken to Omarska? Who was in charge? Who took you?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: In Omarska?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was in a room together with Muslims and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 26th of May, that's your position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you were taken to Keraterm, you said that you were kept in a room with the Serb soldiers. Could you explain as to where this room was?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were there for a day or two, and I think it was the so-called fourth room, fourth, like number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: On the same side where the drug addicts were, but we were taken -- after three or four days, we were taken behind the police because that is where they opened the garage. It was all right except we had a guard with us and we had to go outside to the toilet, but we were together in the same area where the Muslims were except we were not -- we did not communicate because there were bars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my next question was that. Did you -- the time that you spent in this Room 4, were you allowed to go out? Did you see any detainees, non-Serb detainees, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's -- no, no, no. That room was locked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: And they brought us food there. We never went out. We never went out. There was a lavatory inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Room 4, you said that you were taken to another place. As it is not clear, could you tell us where this new place, the prison or the place that you were kept or you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: To the other side of the building where the military police was, to the other side of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it across the road, the Banja Luka-Prijedor road, on to the other side of the building where there was a military barracks?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. The same compound, the same, where those people were detained, except it was on the other side, where the military police was. Where the Prijedor-Banja Luka road, that's on the other side of the road for you and we were on the other side of the building where the military policemen were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said the day that you saw Emsud Bahonjic's body, you were taken to clean the toilets, or were you taken to the toilets?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: To the toilet there because that WC was clogged so that we had to go to the other place, and that was something like a hole, you could relieve yourself, something. It wasn't a proper lavatory. You have to go out. It wasn't a lavatory in the proper sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you left on a Monday and that it was a Sunday that you saw this dead body. Did you see any other prisoners or any other persons near the body during this time?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, because we had no access there. We couldn't get there, nor did we go there. But he was in this hall, lying on a pallet. I didn't really know him. I knew Drago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will stay with Emsud for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: And on that other side were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it that you saw this body of Emsud?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: What time it was? Well, it was afternoon sometime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around what time? Could you be able to help us?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: The 17th or the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know as to what happened to the body thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From how far did you see this body when you saw the body of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Emsud?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come, I came close, two metres, metre and a half. I could see him well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that you knew Drago Tokmadzic quite well. Did you see his body?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any prisoners around it or any guards around it when you saw the body?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: With that guard to take us to relieve ourselves, he showed him to us. But he was already dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this guard who took you out?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Why, Zoran Marijanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the day was it when you saw Drago Tokmadzic's body?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime around noon, after lunch, around 3.00 or half past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was after lunch, is it? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any blood on the body?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was this blood around his head but there were mostly bruises on him. One could see that he had been stricken with some hard objects, because I've been in such predicament too, so I knew what it was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that you saw Zoran Zigic on several occasions at Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Five or six times, I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you could hear him. What exactly did you hear when Zoran Zigic was around the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was always very -- he yelled, he bellowed. He -- just making noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: In uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he carry a weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any weapon. I think he couldn't -- nobody could get through with a weapon. I think he couldn't bring in the rifle because of the guards. Only the guards and their officers could bring in weapons, and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Zoran Zigic when you were detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he would come by. I've said he would bring us cigarettes, alcohol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say as to what happened to his hand?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me, but I heard from these others that during combat -- I don't know, I have no idea. He didn't actually tell me, no. But I know that his hand, his left hand was bandaged, and I don't think he had his index finger. Something like that. And he would keep -- hold his hand up. It was bandaged, and he would hold his hand up under his chin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him as to what position or what authority Zoran had in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just heard from the others that he brought in food and would come with a motorcycle, but nothing official. I didn't know anything about that, and actually I wasn't interested either. He didn't stay long. He just stopped by where we were for 20, 30 minutes, and then would go about his own business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a close relation, your brother-in-law, if I may say so. You didn't ask him as to what position or what authority he had in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this: He was my brother-in-law, yes, but we were also two guys, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him as to what his business was at the camp? Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I can hear you. Yes, I can hear. Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him as to what brought Zoran Zigic to the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I wasn't interested. We weren't as intimate as all that, actually. He lived in quite a different world from me. He moved around in a different crowd. He would act a bit strange when he came by. You could see he was under stress. And then he had separated from his wife. He had his problems. He had two children who were minors, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, while you were staying in the Keraterm camp, did you get to know the guards or the officers at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know as to whether there was a commander?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is the police, the military police, of them who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour, for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during your stay in the camp, did you get to know a person by the name of Zivko Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Deretic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I just have two short questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. Re-examined by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, you said that the military policeman whose name was Tomicic took you into custody after you had wounded him during the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a position to wound him at all in view of the fact -- in view of where you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there so how could I have done that? And hundreds of Muslims can confirm it, can bear out what I say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, do you know the military detention you were in in Keraterm? Did it have anything to do with the detention of the detainees on the front side of the building and locking them up?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Has it got any connection with them?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. That was a separate policeman there. It was all separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one final question --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: The police had to be there. The police had to detain the people who did not want to put a uniform on, so they detained them on that side over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now my final question: After you were brought into the premises of the military police, how many days after that did you see Zigic Zoran, Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the 7th to the 8th up until the 15th, and then he didn't come after that and I asked my guys, "Where's Zigic? I don't see him."

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Deretic. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Gnjatovic, good morning. I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: First, I would like to know your family relationship with Mr. Zigic. As I understood, you were his brother-in-law. That tells me that you were his wife's brother or --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. We married two sisters. Our wives were sisters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The wives were sisters. And he got separated from his wife.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did this create any conflict in the family between you and him?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was different before the war and different after the war, but he was always whimsical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: After this family separation, did this affect your relationship?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really, because I separated from my wife and I left a daughter who was under age but you all your lives to live. He's different from me. I'm different from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that he was all right when he was sober but intolerable when he was drunk. Now, could you just explain this a little bit? How intolerable?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain it. He had a mind of his own. When he had too much to drink, he was a completely different man. A completely different man sober and drunk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Different -- was he aggressive, was he sad, what did he do? Why intolerable? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the situation, who he was with. When he was a taxi driver, he would quarrel with his clients. It would be -- anything would be enough to have this short fuse come to action. He would lose his temper at the slightest provocation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And would he be aggressive?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would he be aggressive then if he lost his temper, physically aggressive?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not really physically aggressive. No, it's difficult for me to explain. But he would be loud generally. And if he was there, he was so boisterous and short-tempered, he would shout. But he wasn't dangerous as into getting into brawls or something. He would, for example, break a glass, turn a table over, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you said during the war he would drink more; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, he did drink and I even heard that he took drugs during the war - I didn't actually see him - marijuana, something like that. I don't use anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you hear about any of his aggressivity during the war, if you said that he drank more?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't actually see him much during the war. I wasn't there. I left in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then how do you know that he drank more?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't see him, but I heard people talking about it, that he was drinking. You know what it's like, rumours. It's different when you see him yourself every day and it's different when you hear other people talk about it, rumours going around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you were taken to Keraterm, you were interrogated by the military police in a room and you could hear interrogation of Muslims in the other room. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, not in that -- the Muslims were interrogated on the other side of the building where there was an investigation department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you did not hear anything? Did you hear them?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't hear anything, no. Just at night, you could hear -- you could hear blows and cries, and of course the camp already existed. I can't say that it didn't when it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean you could hear the blows from the other building?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You could hear the beatings and the moans and the cries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was as loud as that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, depended, depended on the night, but, yes, apart from the shoot -- I can't hear any shooting but you could hear the moans and cries. You know, even an animal, when you beat it, cries out, let alone a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness, I have only one question. You told us how, when you -- the guards were taking you to the toilet, I believe, you saw Emsud Bahonjic one day, on either the 16th or the 17th of June on a pallet. He was already dead. And you saw the bruises on his body. And then a couple of days later, I believe you said June 20th, you saw Drago Tokmadzic also lying on the pallets. My question to you is: Did you have any way of knowing in either case, with either of these people that you saw who were dead for the first time when you saw them lying on the pallets, how long they had been lying there? Did you get a glimpse of them at any other period during that day, or in the case of Bahonjic, any other day? In other words, have any way of knowing how long they were lying out there, dead, on the pallets?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You just saw them that one few moments when the guard took you over or when you went by with the guard in each case?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And you didn't see them again?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm getting some interruption. No, I didn't see them before at all. Just that one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: And later on, they were taken away, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you don't know when they were taken away? Do you know when they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Mr. Gnjatovic, we have no further questions for you. We thank you for coming to testify and wish you a pleasant day.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV GNJATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this brings us to our lunch break. Yes, Ms. Susan Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. I wanted to mention when Mr. Saxon moved in his exhibits, last week there were some exhibits from, I believe it was from Witness DD/5 that both Mr. Deretic and I had identified and the Chamber had gone on to another witness before we had time to move them in. I didn't mention this last week, and I'm not asking that we do it today, but perhaps there might be some opportunity, if we have time at the end of the week, for a Status Conference to review what is outstanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, Ms. Susan Somers, we shall consider that proposal. Let us now adjourn for 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Right. Mr. Deretic, whom do we have now? Is it Mr. Mile Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ivankovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, very well. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, then. You will now read the solemn declaration which Madam Registrar will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now you will answer questions that Mr. Deretic will ask you. Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Examined by Mr. Deretic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can hear you very well, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you be so kind as to tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mile Ivankovic. And I was born -- my father is Dusan and my mother is Mata. I was born on the 12th of September 1948 in Prijedor, and that is where I still live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic, what is your ethnicity and what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat and I am of Catholic faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a highly-skilled car mechanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the war operations started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you involved -- were you engaged in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the 1st Battalion of the 43rd Brigade in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your duty in that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was the commander for the rear operations in that unit, that is, I was a commander of the rear platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic, do you know Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Zoran Zigic very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us more specifically where is it that you live in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: These are the outskirts of Prijedor, and it is called Cirkin Polje. My house is about 2.5 kilometres away from the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your house near Zigic's house?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is across the street. It is four or five metres wide, and my house is right across Mr. Zigic's house. So only a few metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran Zigic's parents?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know them very well. They are true neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are they called?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: They are called Slavka and Nikola.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who arrived there first, your family or Zigic's family, to the place where you live now?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Zigic's came there before us. I came there in 1980 when I bought a plot of land there, and that is when I arrived and I met Zoran's parents; his mother, his father and his grandmother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean then that Zoran grew up in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he grew up in my neighbourhood. He was a very nice guy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he ever played an instrument?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And lots of young people were together with him. They had their yard and young people from the neighbourhood always gathered there and he always respected the neighbours and always showed appreciation for his neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he had a music band that he played in?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did have a band on his own. I don't really know what it was called, The Klas or something. But I know that he played with them. They played at parties in various neighbourhood communities and that is how young people gathered around Zoran Zigic because everybody loved him and held him in high esteem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know at that time did he play in different villages?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they played in Prijedor and around Prijedor. I know that it was precisely in our neighbourhood community in Cirkin Polje that he organised parties where young people from Cirkin Polje gathered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they villages of a specific ethnic structure or were they villages of mixed ethnic population?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, nobody bothered about that. They went around all the villages around Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe to us in a nutshell Zoran Zigic, what kind of a man was he before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that he was a very nice fellow. He was very sociable, very communicative, and all the young people in our neighbourhood community rallied around him. Those youngsters were always with him, and at that time he did not work but whenever he had some money, he'd take them in his car to the town, to a pastry shop or juice or something, and we who lived on the same street, but we were of some -- of an older age, he always respected us. He would always be the first one to greet me, to wish me good morning or good afternoon, always asking about me, about -- and everything. We all respected him no end there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as of the moment, as of the time when you first met Zoran until the time when he was arrested, did you ever notice -- did you ever observe any ethnic tension or a tendency to divide or depreciate among people based on the ethnic origin, or did he mention ever to you as a Croat which ethnic group you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can confirm that, never, ever since the first day I met him to the day when he went to Banja Luka, when he was taken in, he never gave any sign of being a chauvinist or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about his parents?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the question. They are very nice people. His father and his mother, they are true people. They are to this day -- we've had -- we have been -- we are on good terms. We have coffee together. Never, never. For all these 20 odd years that I've known them, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if after the war operation started, whether Zoran Zigic was engaged in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I used to see him in the uniform. He was engaged then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what unit was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I do not know that because there were several units in Prijedor, so that I cannot say which unit he belonged to. I cannot give you a definite answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of a uniform did he wear?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well. He wore a camouflage uniform with a red beret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know therefore in those early days of war in the Prijedor municipality if Zoran was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that very well, when he injured a finger on his left hand, that is his finger was cut, and he was wounded another time somewhere in the area of the chin. He was wounded twice that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean when he sustained injury the first time, at that time, was that hand that you are talking about bandaged?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he had that bandage for a very long time. I remember it well. He had it for two months or so while I was in Prijedor. After that, I left Prijedor too. And I remember when I was saying goodbye to him, when he expressed condolences to me because my father had died, it was on the 18th of August, 1992. He still had it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you met, did he complain to you about that injury?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that he felt pain, that that finger -- in the finger area that he felt how it hurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when both you and Zoran were engaged and when you'd meet, that is, when the war had already broken out, did you sense any change in Zoran Zigic's attitude to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I never sensed it. Out of the question. Far from it. He always behaved decently to me, and he was a right and proper guy always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any of your neighbours complaining against Zoran Zigic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that nobody ever complained, even though we discussed Zoran Zigic and his family because they were in very financial straits because they were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are very sorry but there are interruptions in what we are getting from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war broke out, were there any shortages in the town, of cigarettes, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: There were shortages of everything, but the major problem were liquor and cigarettes because at that time, people were using them a great deal, and I started smoking then. It was the first time that I started smoking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There are interruptions in the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember if at that time, Zoran helped you to find -- to locate cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We'd meet on the street when I came home. We'd stop there and talk and have a cigarette or so and thrash out the problems that we are facing at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I am correct, you told us that your father died on the 18th of August 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. The date is correct. You can check it if you wish, no problem. I buried him on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are not getting the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zoran with you then?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was with us. He was on the street. He was the first one to come to me and express his condolences. And he said to me, "Mile, whatever you need, you just have to ask."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your father was buried the next day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the 19th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 19th of August, 1992. Yes. Yes. Yes. And his parents attended the funeral too. All the inhabitants of the street turned up for the funeral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the funeral, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the front. My unit, that is, went and I went with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that day when you arrived at the front, you mentioned the second wounding of Zoran Zigic. Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do, because I talked with my wife from Modrica and she said that Zoran had been wounded in Gomjenica. He was together with Zeljko Zigic, and that is another neighbour who lives on the same street, perhaps 70 or 80 metres from me and nearer to Zoran's place. That they were together and that Zoran was in luck on that occasion because in Gomjenica, somebody fired, somebody fired and that a bullet scratched Zoran in the area of his chin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the transcript did not reflect the witness's answer to my question. So that I will repeat the question so as to not have to come back to it. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic, I -- when I asked you something, you answered but that was not recorded in the transcript so I will repeat my question. When Zoran came from -- with his family from Pula, how was he?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he had it very hard, you know. He arrived with his parents. His parents had no income at the time, because in the 1990s, his father was retired. But that unfortunate war left them without an income, like everybody else, and he has not managed to regulate it to this day, so that Zoran arrived with his family and he was having it very hard. Over there, he worked and had some means of livelihood, but when they came here, they practically had nothing. But he always laughed. He always smiled. You could never see that he was facing all those difficulties, but we all knew how bad those times were for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zoran's father, Nikola, where did he work? Where did he spend his working life?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: He has worked all his life for Tekol from Maribor. That is a subsidiary in Sisak. And he was a driver for them, and he travelled all over Yugoslavia. That was a company which did house painting and building maintenance, and they worked all over Yugoslavia so that he frequently travelled, but he also came home and that is how I knew him and saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And until when did you used to see Zoran Zigic during that time frame?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him until May 1993. And in June, after the murder -- and I suppose you know about this, about a murder in Prijedor where Zoran was, then he was taken in in the middle of June, and after that, I stopped seeing him because he left to Banja Luka to the detention unit there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, did you change your opinion of Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I've never changed my opinion about him nor will I ever do that. I'll always think all the best of him and his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if, during those days of war, did Zoran change nonetheless, for instance, when it comes to alcohol abuse?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what, he used to drink, he drank even before the war, but within limits, and I would see him often under the influence. But when the war started, of course, people all began to consume more alcohol, much more. So that I often would see him get home and I'd be able to see that he was under the influence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr. Ivankovic: How would you describe Zoran Zigic as a person?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can describe him as my neighbour, outstanding, outstanding man, sociable, friendly. He and his family were really wonderful people at that time, both during the war and before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Ivankovic. Thank you, Mr. President. We have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Deretic. Very well, now, Witness Ivankovic, you will answer the questions the Prosecution will ask you. Mr. Waidyaratne, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We are having the French translation on the English channel. Cross-examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On channel -- we are getting English on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I have no English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only channel 4 seems to be functioning, and we hear English and French on channel 4 at the same time. I think we have to ask somebody in the technical booth to help us. Let us wait a while. Microphone, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [No English translation] ... because what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it all right yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I have no English translation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are on channel 4, Mr. Waidyaratne? Are you on channel 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English is on channel 4. That is what I have on channel 4. On the French channel -- and I don't know where is the French channel because I'm speaking French now. I can hear it in French. Then it must be all right. But it was channel 5. Very well. I think we can now try to move on. Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You may continue. I can hear you in French so it seems the lines are all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said you were mobilised during the conflict. Could you tell us as to where -- and you were attached to the 43rd Brigade. Can you tell us as to where you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, we were deployed in Prijedor at the sports airfield and we provided security for it and I was with the rear unit, taking care of provisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when --

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: And supplying the soldiers who were guarding that sports airfield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Until when was that, from which date to which date?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: From the 16th of -- I was appointed -- I was sent there on the 16th of September, 1991, until the 27th June, 1992. That was when the first battalion where I was the leader was established or when reorganisation took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during this time that you were attached to it, if I'm correct, the Urije position, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, Urije.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 27th of June, where were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: We were assigned to Brezicani, which is a village about eight kilometres away from Prijedor, up in the mountains, to Brezicani, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during these assignments, you will be at these places, given places, and when you get leave, you would come to your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, quite right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you get your leave?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd come home once a week to have a bath and change. You know how it is on the ground; there weren't really proper conditions, so I had to come home to get a change of underwear and to have a bath. And I visited my father often because he was very ill and he lived about three kilometres from my house. That is another locality called Orlovac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can barely hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during this time that you spoke of, you spent very little time in Cirkin Polje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I spent very little time there. I was in the rear. You know what logistics has to do. The most important thing was to supply the army with food, everything that logistics incorporates. So I did that all day and was dead tired in the evening. If I came at night, on duty at night, I would leave in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this time, you did not see Mr. Zoran Zigic very often; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would see him. Not often, no. I did see him around but not often, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not know as to what assignment or as to which -- the work that he did during this time?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivankovic, did you know that Mr. Zoran Zigic was a taxi driver before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew he was a taxi driver before the war. Yes, when he got married and afterwards, he didn't have a means of a livelihood, he didn't work anywhere, so he worked as a taxi driver. He drove a taxi for a time and then he went --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us as to the period which you knew him as a taxi driver?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in 1983, 1982, I can't tell you the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether he drove a taxi before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was 1983 when he was a taxi driver. He drove before the war, yes, in 1983. Not 1990 but 1983, 1983. That was when he was a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic, have you seen him as a taxi driver before the 1992 conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, I apologise for interrupting you, but we have some trouble with the transcript and with the LiveNote. A portion of the LiveNote disappeared from our screens, but I think that everything is under control now so you can continue. If you see something that you need to repeat, or that wasn't entered into the record, I think it will be entered. We can recoup. Is that right, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I've just been informed by the AV section that they had to reset it, but it will be added. The rest of the transcript will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was waiting to hear the French interpretation. There is always an enormous delay between one -- between what is said in the interpretation, but we are on channel 5 now so please continue, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic, you spoke much about Zoran Zigic playing an instrument. Do you know which instrument he played as to who -- whether you know who taught him to play that instrument?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who taught him, but I do know that he played the guitar, and he played it very nicely, exceptionally well. And that's why young people and children all congregated around him because he would go into the yard of his house very often, and his house is opposite my own, and he would play the guitar there. He didn't play indoors, he liked to play outside. He could play several instruments; he played the guitar and I heard later on that he taught his daughter Natasa the synthesizer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic, could you tell us something about your neighbours. Did you have a neighbour by the name of Ivica Sikic?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course it's my neighbour. He lives about 50 to 70 metres away from me. Not more than that. Sikic Ivica and his wife Soka. Soka is his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you often visit Zoran Zigic and his family, especially his father's house?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would go across. If there were any problems, we'd talk about it. Usually we would go over to have a cup of coffee, say hello, have a chat, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Zoran Zigic and family was not on very strong financial position during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can just imagine the father had no income at all. The mother had no pension or anything like that. Zoran wasn't working anywhere, neither was his wife. He had two lovely daughters, Sanja and Natasa, so you can understand what situation he was in. It wasn't easy for him, that's all I can say, because there was a shortage of everything. And his house is on a plot of land that is 600 square metres so it was a small plot of land. If they had something growing in the garden, they would pick it, dig up a few potatoes, carrots, beans that they had in their yard, and that's what they lived on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivankovic, now after a detailed description of the last answer, did you ask Mr. Zoran Zigic as to where he got the cigarettes that you spoke about, from where he got those provisions?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody, people had cigarettes. Somebody always had cigarettes. I got some in the unit I was in, but very small quantities. People smoked a lot. I never actually asked him, but he would offer me a cigarette. From time to time, we would smoke a cigarette together but I never asked him where he actually got the cigarettes from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zoran Zigic at any time tell you that he was able to get cigarettes and that he took cigarettes to the Keraterm camp to be sold and to be given to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. He never said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke about some information that you got from your wife about the injury that Mr. Zoran Zigic sustained. Did your wife tell you as to who was with Zoran Zigic the time that he was injured?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was our neighbour's small boy, his name is Zeljko Sikic, and he might have been about 13 years old at the time. He was a young boy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your father died on the 18th of August and that you buried him on the 19th and then, thereafter, that you left. Did Mr. Zoran Zigic come to the funeral on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear you very well now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MILE IVANKOVIC
